video_title: Worry List Is Growing More Worrisome
gist: Ed Yardeni's Monday call, recorded just after returning from vacation, argues a Middle East escalation (IRGC proxies/Houthis threatening Red Sea transit) has pushed oil above $100 toward $110, driven the 10-year Treasury yield back to 5%, and boxed in both Fed Chair Kevin Warsh and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent — he expects a 25bp rate HIKE at the coming FOMC and possibly a hiking cycle. He keeps his S&P 500 year-end target at 8,400 (now 425 of 2026 EPS times a 19.7 multiple) because forward earnings and revenues keep making record highs, but raises his subjective odds of a bearish/recessionary outcome from 20% to 30%, flags energy as the obvious overweight hedge, and expects a pullback or ~10% correction rather than a bear market.

themes.theme: Fed Turns to Hiking Under Warsh

insights.claim: Ed Yardeni expects Fed Chair Kevin Warsh to deliver a 25 basis point rate HIKE at the upcoming FOMC meeting, and to signal at the press conference that this may not be one-and-done but the start of a hiking cycle of another one or two increases.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: A hiking Fed inverts the consensus easing trade — front-end duration, rate-sensitive equities and carry strategies are all positioned for the wrong direction if this is right.
insights.quote: I think uh Borsch will deliver a 25% uh rate hike um at the FOMC meeting. I think he will at the press conference uh remain hawkish about inflation

insights.claim: The two-year Treasury yield is currently signaling three rate hikes over the next 12 to 24 months, which would fully reverse the prior year's 75 basis points of cuts.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: The front end is already pricing a full reversal of the easing cycle — a useful market-implied benchmark to judge whether the Fed is behind or ahead of the curve.
insights.quote: now the two-year is signaling three rate hikes uh over let's say the next 12 to 24 months which would reverse the rate cuts that we had uh last year

insights.claim: Yardeni argues the Fed's 100bp of cuts in 2024 and 75bp in 2025 were never justified by a resilient full-employment economy with inflation still above 2%, and that the bond market validated that view by sending yields up 100 basis points after the first round of cuts.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Establishes the analytical frame that easing into a strong economy raises rather than lowers long yields — the same mechanism now working against any dovish Fed surprise.
insights.quote: a drop in interest rates by 100 basis points uh wasn't justified by the uh what we viewed as a resilient economy with an inflation rate that wasn't uh yet close to 2%

insights.claim: Warsh lost credibility with markets by talking hawkish in June and July press conferences without acting, which pushed the two-year yield to price tightening on its own in a classic bond vigilante move.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: When a central bank's rhetoric and action diverge, the market prices the tightening itself — watch the 2-year rather than the dot plot for the effective policy stance.
insights.quote: if he was going to talk like a hawk then he had to walk like a hawk or at least fly like a hawk

insights.claim: Warsh's no-forward-guidance, let-the-markets-tell-us approach has become a trap because markets are now loudly demanding that the Fed get ahead of inflation and raise rates.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: If the Fed is market-reactive by design, market pricing becomes self-fulfilling policy — rate expectations are the variable to watch, not Fed speak.
insights.quote: the markets are screaming at the Fed and have been screaming of late that uh they should get ahead of the inflation problem and raise rates

insights.claim: A surprise 50 basis point Fed hike would likely push the 10-year Treasury yield DOWN rather than up, because bond vigilantes want proof the Fed is vigilant about inflation.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: A counterintuitive long-duration setup: the most aggressive hike would be the bullish outcome for long bonds, inverting the naive rates-up-yields-up trade.
insights.quote: I think if they did 50 base points I think the bond yield would actually come down. Uh I think that's what the bond vigilantes the bond vigilantes want to see

insights.claim: Yardeni dismisses the chatter among some economists that Warsh should hike 50 basis points, judging that Warsh's head is not in that direction and that a 50bp move would cause President Trump's head to explode given Trump's public demand for lower rates.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Political friction between the White House and a hiking Fed is an under-priced volatility source for rates and the dollar into the meeting.

themes.theme: Oil Shock as the Critical Variable

insights.claim: Houthi advances toward controlling the strait in and out of the Red Sea have driven oil above $100 and toward $110, with Goldman Sachs analysts talking about $120 oil.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: A concrete price path and a named sell-side target give a reference band for energy equity and inflation-breakeven positioning.
insights.quote: the folks over at Goldman Sachs have I think a few last week talked about $120 oil and we're certainly over 100 and uh approaching 110

insights.claim: Yardeni identifies the price of oil as the single critical variable driving the entire macro complex right now, because higher-for-longer oil seeps into inflation data and puts the Fed in a box.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Makes crude the master variable for the rates and equity outlook — a de-escalation in the Middle East is the fastest path to relief across all assets.
insights.quote: now, of course, um driving all this is the price of oil. That's that's really the the critical variable here here.

insights.claim: The prior oil selloff during Middle East de-escalation revealed how much physical oil actually exists in the world, meaning the current spike is a geopolitical risk premium that can unwind as quickly as it appeared.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Frames the oil move as premium rather than scarcity — argues against chasing crude and for treating energy as a hedge rather than a secular long.
insights.quote: when the war simmerred down and uh deescalated and there was some diplomacy going on uh we saw how much oil there really was in the world and the price of oil came tumbling down

insights.claim: Iran's IRGC remains in control and its proxy network is intact and coordinated, which Yardeni treats as the structural reason the Middle East risk is not a one-off headline.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Argues the geopolitical risk premium in oil and bonds is persistent rather than transient, favoring sustained hedges over tactical fades.

themes.theme: Bond Yields at 5% and Treasury's Bazooka

insights.claim: Yardeni's framework puts the normal range for the 10-year Treasury yield at 4% to 5%, with the current 5% level sitting at the very top of that range and likely to move higher absent a policy response.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Gives an explicit level-based framework: 5% is the range top, so duration buyers need a policy catalyst rather than mean reversion alone.
insights.quote: we still think that the normal range for the 10-year bond yield is four to 5%. But clearly we're at the top of that range right now.

insights.claim: Elevated interest rates at current levels are a healthy sign of a very strong US economy rather than a malfunction, contradicting the White House view that a best-in-world economy deserves the lowest rates.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Reframes rising yields as a growth signal, which supports equity earnings even as it pressures multiples — the opposite of a stagflation read.
insights.quote: interest rates around current levels in many ways are a healthy sign. They're a sign that the US economy is very doing very very well

insights.claim: Yardeni thinks Bessent should consider pulling out the bazooka — shifting Treasury issuance toward bills instead of bonds, the same maneuver Janet Yellen used in 2023 that Bessent himself had criticized.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: A concrete, watchable policy catalyst: a quarterly refunding shift toward bills would be the signal to cover long-bond shorts.
insights.quote: I think uh Bessant u has to consider pulling out the bazooka.

insights.claim: Yardeni notes that when Yellen made the more-bills announcement on November 1st 2023 the bond market calmed after the 10-year had touched 5% intraday in late October, but warns the setup is worse now because inflation was falling then while persistence of inflation and deficits is the focus today.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Tempers expectations that a repeat of the 2023 bills maneuver would work as well — the same playbook may deliver a weaker bond rally this time.

insights.claim: The unwinding yen carry trade may be the main explanation for why bond yields are rising around the world, as Japan raises rates and a stronger yen removes the near-zero-cost funding that financed foreign bond purchases in Brazil and the United States.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Identifies a global flow driver independent of US fundamentals — Japanese rate policy and yen strength become leading indicators for global term premia.
insights.quote: that may be a good reason good explanation uh maybe the main explanation for why bond yields around the world have been been going up

insights.claim: Bessent's intervention on behalf of the yen was motivated by preventing Japanese selling of US Treasuries to support their currency, and it unnerved rather than calmed markets.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Reveals that official FX action is really about protecting the Treasury bid — failed interventions signal escalating stress in the foreign demand base for US debt.

insights.claim: Bessent's original pitch that administration policies would deliver more productivity, lower inflation and more real growth — effectively signing on to the Roaring 2020s scenario — is now undermined by oil prices and tariffs both pushing inflation higher.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: The policy credibility that anchored long-end expectations is eroding, which is the mechanism for further term-premium expansion.

insights.claim: Yardeni says the TIPS yield has contributed much of the rise to 5% on the bond yield and admits he does not have a clean read on what the TIPS yield is signaling, though of late he thinks it reflects the economy's strength.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: A real-yield-led selloff (rather than breakeven-led) argues the move is growth-driven, which is less damaging to earnings than an inflation-scare selloff.
insights.quote: for the life of me, if anybody's got a really good handle on what the tips yield actually means, that would be helpful

themes.theme: Worry List and Rising Recession Odds

insights.claim: Yardeni Research raised its subjective probability of a bearish outcome from 20% to 30%, cutting the Roaring 2020s base case from 80% to 70%, and treats that bearish probability as effectively its odds of a recession in the foreseeable future.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: A quantified, trackable sentiment gauge from a prominent bull — further moves to 40% or 50% would be the tell that the target itself is coming down.
insights.quote: we went from 20% to 30% as the uh the risk that it that things will not go well for the base case. And so the base case goes from 80% to 70%. That's my way of communicating that guess what I'm worried.

insights.claim: Yardeni signals his own forward guidance: if he raises the bearish probability to 40% or 50%, he will have to start lowering the S&P 500 target, because the probability is losing confidence in the base case.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Gives a specific trigger to watch from a widely followed strategist — a move to 40% would mark the turn in street targets.

insights.claim: The best real-time recession warning indicators to watch are weekly initial unemployment claims and weekly Redbook same-store retail sales on the consumer side, plus company guidance in the coming earnings season on the capital spending side.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: A concrete weekly-frequency dashboard for front-running the official data on recession risk.

insights.claim: Small-cap relative performance is a useful gauge of the market's perception of recession risk because small caps are especially sensitive to recession fears.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Russell-vs-S&P relative strength becomes a live market-implied recession probability, complementing the macro data.
insights.quote: Small caps tend to be especially sensitive to fears of of a recession.

insights.claim: Yardeni maintains there will be no recession, noting the Roaring 2020s thesis has survived the most widely anticipated recession of all time and that three years remain in the decade.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Anchors the constructive case: absent a recession, analyst estimates historically hold and equities grind higher through the noise.
insights.quote: we've had the most widely anticipated recession of all times that just didn't happen uh so far

insights.claim: Yardeni had always expected that the main risk to his bullish scenario would be geopolitical in nature, with the second-order chain running from geopolitics to inflation to fiscal concerns.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Defines the transmission channel to monitor: geopolitical shocks matter to equities only insofar as they move inflation and then the fiscal/bond picture.

insights.claim: Yardeni Research is keeping its S&P 500 year-end target at 8,400 and has raised its year-end earnings estimate from $415 to $425 per share, implying a 19.7 multiple instead of the prior 20.2 on $415.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: The exact EPS-times-multiple arithmetic behind a street target lets investors stress-test it directly against their own multiple assumptions.
insights.quote: 425 * 19.7 multiple uh gives us 8,400

insights.claim: Consensus 2027 S&P 500 earnings expectations have risen to a record $419.54, up from $415 only a few weeks earlier, and Yardeni considers $425 realistic by year-end.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Rising rather than falling forward estimates is the load-bearing support for equities in a rising-rate environment; a stall here breaks the bull case.
insights.quote: we're at $41,9.54 on the 20 27 number. That's uh pretty impressive.

insights.claim: This bull market is unusual because analyst earnings expectations keep rising rather than being cut into earnings season, a pattern Yardeni labels FEMO — fabulous earnings momentum.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Inverts the usual playbook where stocks rise despite estimate cuts — investors should watch for the regime to revert to the historical pattern of downward revisions.
insights.quote: It's been FIMO fabulous earnings momentum

insights.claim: The mark-to-market capital gains that flattered forward earnings came from only two or three companies and are reflected in the 2026 number, while forward earnings are now converging toward 2027 estimates that exclude mark-to-market forecasts.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Means the current earnings strength is cleaner than headline forward EPS suggests — a rebuttal to the argument that index earnings are inflated by non-operating gains.

insights.claim: Analysts' long-term growth expectations have hit an all-time record of 26.7% annual earnings growth over the next 3 to 5 years, which Yardeni calls impossible and explicit irrational exuberance even though it is grounded in genuinely strong recent earnings.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: A named sentiment extreme from a bull — bottom-up long-term growth expectations at records are a classic late-cycle warning even while near-term estimates hold.
insights.quote: there's no way that earnings are going to grow 26.7% on an annual basis over the next 3 to 5 years

insights.claim: Forward revenues continue to make new highs despite the Russia-Ukraine war, the Middle East situation, higher oil and rising yields, and Yardeni treats forward revenues as a proxy for global rather than merely US revenues.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Makes S&P forward revenues a usable real-time global growth indicator — its continued strength contradicts the geopolitical-slowdown narrative.

insights.claim: Forward profit margins for the S&P 500 stand at 16.8%, with year-over-year growth of forward earnings per share and forward revenues per share both remaining extremely strong and net earnings revisions still positive.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Provides the specific margin and revisions levels whose deterioration would mark the actual turn in the earnings cycle.

insights.claim: Yardeni's mechanism for this bull market is that forward earnings rise faster than the forward P/E falls, so the index advances even as the multiple compresses.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Reframes multiple compression as compatible with rising prices, which matters for how investors interpret de-rating in a rising-rate regime.
insights.quote: forward earnings continues to uh go up. Uh the forward PE continues to go down. Uh and uh the market goes up uh because on balance forward earnings go up faster than the the PE goes down.

insights.claim: Yardeni rejects being labeled the most bullish strategist on the street, arguing the sell-side analysts themselves are more bullish than his 8,400 target.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Suggests bottom-up consensus is running ahead of top-down targets — a positioning asymmetry that amplifies downside if guidance disappoints.
insights.quote: the feedback I was getting is that we were the most bullish on the street and my response was no we're not uh the analysts are the most bullish on the street

insights.claim: Yardeni argues analysts will not cut S&P 500 EPS estimates over the AI-pacing controversy so far, because analysts take their cue from company guidance and companies have kept saying things are hanging in there.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Company guidance, not AI narrative shifts, is the actual trigger for estimate cuts — watch the guidance calls rather than the AI debate.

themes.theme: AI Regulation and the Capex Paradox

insights.claim: Yardeni frames the sudden AI-doom narrative as coming from the AI industry itself, which would not mind regulation, raising the prospect of regulatory capture where the industry guides the regulators.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: If incumbents shape AI rules, regulation becomes a moat rather than a cost — favoring large incumbents over challengers and open-source competitors.
insights.quote: whether the AI industry wants the government to regulate them and then the AI industry will capture the regulators and kind of guide things the way they want them to go

insights.claim: A specific goal of the US AI industry in seeking regulation is to put limits or restraints on the open-source models coming out of China.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Identifies Chinese open-source models as the competitive threat driving US AI policy — a direct read on pricing power for closed-model vendors.

insights.claim: Yardeni predicts the US and China will converge on the need for more AI guardrails and some coordination between the two countries, against President Trump's full-bore, don't-regulate-because-China-won't position.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: US-China AI coordination would reset the race-to-the-bottom assumption embedded in AI capex forecasts and chip demand.

insights.claim: Yardeni argues the market no longer knows what it is rooting for on AI — a slowdown in AI capex would hurt the growth narrative but would also stop depleting free cash flow and could help corporate profits.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Names the two-sided AI trade explicitly: a capex slowdown is bearish for suppliers but bullish for hyperscaler cash flow, so the sign of the equity impact depends on where you sit in the chain.
insights.quote: if that suddenly slows, shouldn't that be a positive? Uh wouldn't that be a good good thing for corporate cash flow or maybe even uh corporate profits?

insights.claim: Yardeni agrees that if AI spending slows, bond yields could drop because of less crowding out, which would in turn boost the equity multiple.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Supplies a hedge rationale: an AI capex disappointment might be partially offset for the index by lower rates and multiple expansion.
insights.quote: If AI spending slows, could bond yields drop as there is less of a crowding out effect and that could boost the multiple? The answer is sure.

insights.claim: Yardeni characterizes the market's stance toward AI as having moved past AI fatigue into total confusion and head-spinning reaction to developments in the AI marketplace.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Unanchored positioning in the most crowded theme implies larger two-way volatility in AI-linked names on each headline.
insights.quote: for a while there I've been saying that the market has AI fatigue. Uh now I'm not sure what the market has with regards to AI total confusion

themes.theme: Positioning: Energy Hedge and Correction Playbook

insights.claim: Yardeni Research has been overweight energy for a while, the S&P 500 energy sector is outperforming as oil rises, and Yardeni calls energy the obvious overweight to hold as a hedge against the current geopolitical and inflation developments.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: An explicit, currently-working sector hedge recommendation tied directly to the Red Sea oil risk.
insights.quote: we think uh energy is probably the is the obvious uh overweight position to have as a hedge against all these uh developments of late

insights.claim: With the S&P 500 not far off its all-time high, Yardeni expects a pullback that could turn into a roughly 10% correction, but not a bear market unless the current pressures produce a recession — and he views such a correction as creating buying opportunities.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Sets a magnitude and a rule: buy the 10% drawdown unless the recession evidence actually shows up in claims and guidance.
insights.quote: I don't think this is going to be a bare market. Uh this could be a a 10% correction. Uh I suppose u but I think it will create buying opportunities

insights.claim: Yardeni expects bull-bear sentiment ratios to turn sharply bearish over the next couple of weeks, consistent with September's history as a tough month that sometimes spills into October.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: A contrarian sentiment washout in a seasonally weak window is exactly the setup his buy-the-correction rule is designed to exploit.
insights.quote: I would not be surprised to see the bull bear ratios turning very bearish very coming down sharply over the next couple of weeks

insights.claim: If the correction deepens, Yardeni expects a total market takedown rather than a rotation out of tech into value, healthcare and staples, despite the broadening rotation into equal-weight S&P 500 and small caps seen earlier in the year.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Warns that defensive rotation will not protect capital in this drawdown — correlations go to one, so cash or hedges beat sector rotation.
insights.quote: I I think it probably more of a total takedown than rotation.

insights.claim: Yardeni sees no immediate relief for the bond market from fundamentals because neither a sudden weakening in the economy nor a sudden drop in inflation is in the cards, leaving the outcome dependent on whether Bessent and Warsh coordinate a policy response.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Makes policy coordination, not data, the binary catalyst for bonds — position around the FOMC and Treasury announcements rather than around macro prints.
insights.quote: doesn't look to me as though that there's any uh immediate relief coming from the from the fundamentals
